The distinction between applications to strike based on an allegation that no cause of action exists at law and those based on an allegation that the case is hopeless on the facts was again noted by the Court of Appeal: The Alberta Court of Appeal in German v. Major[(1985), 39 Alta. L.R. (2d) 270 (C.A.)] stressed that where the defendant suggests that there is no such cause of action known to the law, i.e., that the plaintiff's lawsuit is bad in law or the defendant has a clear legal defence, then the court must assume the truth of the facts in the statement of claim. But the Court of Appeal said it was different where the defendants contend that the lawsuit is hopeless factually, and thus frivolous and vexatious. The test is whether it is “plain and obvious that the action cannot succeed.”Zurich Investments Ltd. v. Excelsior Life Insurance Co. (1988), 59 Alta. L.R. (2d) 209 at 211 (C.A.). In Estrin v. Law Society (Alberta) (1995), 35 Alta. L.R. (3d) 153 (C.A.), the court commented on “hopeless” cases. At p. 157 the court said: The case will not be hopeless in point of fact where plaintiff can point to some evidence to support the essential allegations of fact. In Temilini v. Ontario Provincial Police Commissioner (1990), 73 O.R. (2d) 664 (C.A.), Grange J.A. drew the following distinction at p. 670: … I concede that the plaintiff should not enter litigation purely on a ‘fishing expedition’ but the distinction between that and using the processes such as production or discovery to supplement a case already based on some evidence is a fine one. It is sufficient to say that a plaintiff who asserts a proper cause of action where there is some evidence upon which the case can be built should not be foreclosed. 27. If the Action Will Be Tried in Any Event The court should be loath to strike out a portion of a claim where the matter is to go to trial in any case. In Sentinel Review Co. v. Robinson, [1927] 2 D.L.R. 60, at p. 63 Meredith, C.J.C.P., overturned a Master who had struck certain portions of a defence using these words: It is manifestly better, when it can be done without prejudice to the interests of either party, that all questions in one action should be considered at one time by one court, thereby avoiding possible conflict of opinion and certain delay and needless costs. Where a pleading is manifestly bad and is embarrassing, an officer at Chambers, as well as a judge at Chambers, has power to strike out the pleading, but, it should not be necessary to add, that powers should be exercised only in plain cases. There is always some danger of a pruner cutting off a fruitful bough mistaking it for an unfruitful one. Lamont, J., in Canadian Grain Co. v. Lepp (1916), 35 W.L.R. 688, at p. 690 expresses a similar sentiment: Where, however, as here, after striking out the paragraphs which may be properly struck out, the plaintiff has to go to trial to prove his entire case, I do not see that any good purpose would be served by striking out any of these paragraphs. I agree with the remarks of Ritchie, J., in Holmes v. Taylor, supra, where he said: ‘If the cause is to go to trial, it had better go with the defence unmutilated.’ This rule was never intended to afford the plaintiff the opportunity of trying the case piecemeal. The object of the rule was to prevent the delay and expense of an unreal defence. I do not wish to be understood as holding that under no circumstances should a portion of a defence be struck out, but, generally speaking, but little will be gained by striking out an individual paragraph where the plaintiff has to go to court to prove his case. If he has material sufficient to justify a court in striking out the paragraph it will usually be found sufficient to establish his allegation at the trial. At any rate, the rules relating to admissions of facts for use at the trial afford the plaintiff ample protection. In essence I must be satisfied that striking the offending paragraphs in no way imperils the statement of claim as a whole. Murphy v. Kenting Drilling Co. (1996), 190 A.R. 77 (Master), at pp. 79-80, per Master Waller. Master Waller's statement that “the court should be loathe to strike out a portion of a claim where the matter is to go to trial in any case” was quoted with approval by Russell, J.A. in Decock v. Alberta, 2000 ABCA 122, 2000 CarswellAlta 384, 255 A.R. 234, 79 Alta. L.R. (3d) 11; leave to appeal allowed (2000) 293 A.R. 388 (note) (S.C.C.), at p. 260 (notice of discontinuance filed September 10, 2001). 28. Rule Applies to Provincial Court I should mention that it was argued by the plaintiff that a judge of the Provincial Court of Alberta has no inherent power to strike out pleadings However, s. 19.1(2) of the Provincial Court Act provides that: (2) Where this Act or the regulations do not provide for a specific practice or procedure of the court that is necessary to ensure an expeditious and inexpensive resolution of a matter before the Court, the Court may (a) apply the Alberta Rules of Court, and (b) modify the Alberta Rules of Court as needed. Therefore, I find that the Provincial Court Judge had jurisdiction to strike out the pleading. Parker v. Menzies Field Mechanical Services Ltd. (1998), 226 A.R. 204 (Q.B.), at 208, per Coutu J. 29. Standard of Review on Appeal From an Old Rule 129 (current Rule 3.68) Order Decisions on applications to strike are owed a high level of deference by this court. Orders made under rule 129 are discretionary and appellate courts should only reverse if “it is obvious without elaborate argument that there is no cause of action”: Kvaerner Enviropower Inc. v. Tanar Industries Ltd. et al. (1998), 223 A.R. 348, 183 W.A.C. 348 (C.A.), at 352 (C.A.). The scope of review for decisions under rule 129 is limited to a determination whether: (i) the decision was unreasonable because no weight or insufficient weight was given to relevant considerations; or (ii) the chambers judge erred in law: Decock et al. v. Alberta et al. (2000), 255 A.R. 234, 220 W.A.C. 234 at 240 (C.A.). First Mortgage Alberta Fund (V) Inc. et al. v. Boychuk et al. (2002), 312 A.R. 1 (C.A.) at 3-4, per curiam.

Rule 3.68(2)—Non-disclosure of action or defence See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.68(2). 1. What Is a Cause of Action? A cause of action is a set of facts which, if established, would entitle the plaintiff to some form of relief. Scotia Mortgage Corp. v. Goss (1987), 83 A.R. 15 at 18 (Master). 2. Test In Rudichuk v. Genesis Land Development Corp., 2019 ABQB 132, 2019 CarswellAlta 336, Madam Justice Marriott gave this summary of the law as it relates to applications to strike a claim on the basis that it does not disclose a reasonable claim: [8] Rule 3.68(1)(a) and (2)(b) provide that all or part of a claim may be struck out where it “discloses no reasonable claim”. As established by the Supreme Court of Canada, it is accepted that a court should only strike a claim if it is plain and obvious that the pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action: Hunt v T&N plc, 1990 CanLII 90 (SCC), [1990] 2 SCR 959 and Knight v Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd, 2011 SCC 42 (CanLII). It is only if a claim has no reasonable prospect of success, then it should be struck, and so long as the plaintiff has some chance of success and the claim is arguable, then the Court should allow the matter to proceed to trial: Hunt at 989; Imperial Tobacco at para 17. [9] Further, the Supreme Court of Canada has held that it is not determinative that the law has not yet recognized a particular claim and a court should be generous and err on the side of permitting a novel, but arguable claim to proceed to trial: Imperial Tobacco at para 21. Thus, the statement of claim should be struck “only if it is clear that in law the case cannot succeed, based on principles directly applicable to the case as set out in the pleadings”: Anger v Berkshire Investment Group Inc, 2001 CanLII 24141 (ON CA), [2001] OJ No 379 (CA) at para 15. [10] When applying this test, the Court may examine a number of factors, including the clarity of the factual pleadings and the existence of case law discussing similar causes of action: NEP Canada ULC v MEC OP LLC, 2014 ABCA 140 (CanLII) at para 16. However, the parties may not submit new evidence on this application: Rules, r 3.68(3). In considering the claim, the court must assume that the facts as pleaded are true: Hunt at 980. Finally, the defendant bears the burden of proof on this application, and the onus to meet is “extremely high”: Alberta Adolescent Recovery Centre v CBC, 2012 ABQB 48 (CanLII) at para 29. … [13] On an application to strike a claim when the issue in question is duty of care, the court need not determine “whether a duty of care will be recognized, but whether it is plain and obvious that no duty of care can be recognized”: Haskett v Equifax Canada Inc (2003), 2003 CanLII 32896 (ON CA), 63 OR (3d) 577 (CA) at para 24. In Alexander v. Pacific Trans-Ocean Resources Ltd. (1991), 115 A.R. 317 (Q.B.), at 318-19, [; affirmed (1992) 120 A.R. 22 (C.A.)], Justice Perras said: As well, I keep in mind the admonition of Wilson, J., in Hunt v. T & N plc et al. (1990), 117 N.R. 321 (S.C.C.), when she said at pp. 345-346: Thus, the test in Canada governing the application of provisions like rule 19(24)(a) of the British Columbia Rules of Court is the same as the one that governs an application under R.S.C., Order 18, r. 19: assuming that the facts as stated in the statement of claim can be proved, is it ‘plain and obvious’ that the plaintiff's statement of claim discloses no reasonable cause of action? As in England, if there is a chance that the plaintiff might succeed, then the plaintiff should not be ‘driven from the judgment seat’. Neither the length and complexity of the issues, the novelty of the cause of action, nor the potential for the defendant to present a strong defence should prevent the plaintiff from proceeding with his or her case. Only if the action is certain to fail because it contains a radical defect ranking with the others listed in rule 19(24) of the British Columbia Rules of Court should the relevant portions of a plaintiff's statement of claim be struck out under rule 19(24)(a). It is noted that r. 19(24)(a) of the British Columbia Supreme Court is for all intents and purposes the same as r. 129(1)(a) of the Alberta Rules of Court. The same test was adapted by Wachowich J. in Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. v. Prisco (1990), 115 A.R. 184 at 187-88 (Q.B.). In Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959, Wilson J., speaking for the court, said at p. 344: Indeed, I would go so far as to suggest that where a statement of claim reveals a difficult and important point of law, it may well be critical that the action be allowed to proceed. Only in this way can we be sure that the common law in general, and the law of torts in particular, will continue to evolve to meet the legal challenges that arise in our modern industrial society. In Hirtz v. Alberta (Public Trustee) (1997), 221 A.R. 324 (Q.B.), at pp. 335-36, Moreau J. specifically quoted the above-noted passage from Wilson J.'s judgment in Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959. And Fruman J. has provided the following summary of the applicable principles: The principles which apply in respect of a motion to strike out pleadings have been stated in many cases and do not seem to be at issue in these proceedings. In Hunt v. T & N plc, (sub nom. Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.) [1990] 6 W.W.R. 385 (S.C.C.), Wilson J. summarized the relevant principles. At p. 400, she stated that the Supreme Court of Canada has consistently upheld the “plain and obvious” test. At p. 401, she phrased the question as follows: “… assuming that the facts as stated in the statement of claim can be proved, is it ‘plain and obvious’ that the plaintiff's statement of claim discloses no reasonable cause of action?” She confirms that: Neither the length and complexity of the issues, the novelty of the cause of action, nor the potential for the defendant to present a strong defence should prevent the plaintiff from proceeding with his or her case. Only if the action is certain to fail because it contains a radical defect … should the relevant portions of a plaintiff's statement of claim be struck … Wilson J. confirms that an application to strike pleadings is not an appropriate forum in which to engage in a detailed examination of the strengths and weaknesses of the plaintiff's case. One is to assume that all facts alleged by the plaintiff are true, and then determine whether the plaintiff can present a question “fit to be tried”. Wilson J. considered other Supreme Court of Canada decisions and indicated that following these decisions “the test remained whether the outcome of the case was ‘plain and obvious’ or ‘beyond reasonable doubt’”. I believe that this summary of the principles is also an enumeration of the principles used in Alberta in connection with a motion to strike under R. 129 …Rocky Mountain Rail Society v. H & D Hobby Distributing Ltd. (1995), 27 Alta. L.R. (3d) 424 at 427-28 (Q.B.). Madam Justice Fruman then drew a distinction between “novel legal propositions” (which normally are not to be struck) and “broadening a narrowly defined tort” (which might be struck). At p. 431 of Rocky Mountain Rail Society, her Ladyship said: While judges should not be quick to strike pleadings which raise novel legal propositions, I do not see this matter as a novel proposition but rather as a broadening of a narrowly defined tort. No public policy reasons have been suggested to justify such an extension, which would open the floodgates of this type of pleading and would put Rocky Mountain and its directors to the time and expense of defending an action that is doomed to failure. In Manulife Financial Services Ltd. v. BTK Holdings Ltd. (1997), 56 Alta. L.R. (3d) 355 (Master), Master Funduk noted that “novel” does not encompass “far-fetched”. At p. 360, the learned Master said: It also does not help to say that a pleading should not be struck out where it raises something novel. Novel does not encompass something that is plain and obvious beyond doubt. The answer to that (said in another context) is: It is true that in one decision I said the test is what is arguable. It must be understood, of course, that that means reasonably arguable. In a sense almost any proposition (except maybe whether two plus two equals four) is arguable. But it cannot be a far-fetched argument; it cannot be an argument that is contrary to binding authority. (Mocyk v. Municipal District of East Peace No. 131 (Oct. 10, 1995), C.A. 9503-0257-A.C., Côté J.A.) Novel does not encompass far-fetched. The Court of Appeal in Korte v. Deloitte, Haskins & Sells (1993), 8 Alta. L.R. (3d) 337, 1993 CarswellAlta 304, 135 A.R. 389 (C.A.), noted that specific words need not be pleaded to set forth a cause of action—the test is whether the essence of the cause of action is set forth in the pleading. At p. 340, the court said: The court should also allow for some generosity in assessing whether the statement of claim discloses a cause of action, and it is not always necessary to plead specific words or specific legal conclusions providing that the essence of the action is outlined in the pleadings. In Tanar Industries Ltd. v. American Home Assurance Co. (1998), 64 Alta. L.R. (3d) 144 (C.A.), the Court of Appeal noted that if a chambers judge dismisses an application under R. 129(1)(a), an appeal ought to be allowed only if it is obvious that there is no cause of action. At p. 147, the court, per curiam, said: In addition, this Court must have regard to the standard of review that is relevant in appeals of this sort. Appellate courts will not lightly interfere with discretionary orders such as those made under Rule 129(1) … Moreover, in our view, when a chambers judge dismisses a motion to strike out a statement of claim, an appellate court should reverse him or her only if it is obvious without elaborate argument that there is no cause of action. 3. Alleging Negligence Equates to Alleging Fact The plaintiff alleges that the City owed a duty to her, that it breached that duty and that she suffered damages. For pleadings purposes, an allegation of negligence in a pleading is considered to be an allegation of fact: Fullowha v. Whitford (Nov. 25, 1996), C.A. 00628-C.A.00634 (N.W.T. C.A.). The court says: All of the defendants who moved argue that the amended statement of claim at key places offers something bald and without supporting detail. Some counsel allege that these are bald facts, others that they are bald conclusions. Doubtless a statement of claim must plead the necessary facts, and a mere legal conclusion is not enough. Merely to plead that the defendant is liable to the plaintiff for the tort of defamation might well not suffice, for example. That is a legal conclusion, not a fact. However, there is a big difference between pleading a mere conclusion of law and pleading a fact. To plead that the defendant negligently injured the plaintiff is to plead a fact, even if it also implies a legal conclusion… . . . . . The reasons under appeal also say that ‘Allegations which are nothing more than speculative assumptions disguised as facts are also unacceptable.’ They cite no authority for that, and we know of none. If a plaintiff pleads facts, she need not have any evidence of them. She may rely on later discovery or cross-examination at trial to yield them. A plaintiff who is knocked unconscious in a traffic accident and suffers temporary amnesia may know nothing about the accident. All of her statement of claim may be speculative assumptions. But no one would strike it out on that ground, and her speculations may well be proved accurate at the trial… . . . . . And it is customary to plead particulars of negligence, though no rule requiring that was shown to us… . . . . . Can one logically say that a statement of claim which pleads the facts which give a cause of action discloses no cause of action, because it does not give the details of when, where, or how? We reject that suggestion, and these cases agree: Paterson & Hidson v. Livingstone, [1931] 1 D.L.R. 386 (S.C.C.); Bechtel Can. v. Stearns Catalytic, [1990] A.U.D. 212, 215 (C.A.); cf. Baxter v. Calgary Sexual Assault Centre (10 Jan ‘95), Calg. # 14546 (Alta. C.A.)… The following quote, from Fullowha is a complete answer to the suggestion that insufficient facts are pled: In any event, the simple answer is that the Rules and the decided cases say that a claim should be struck out only for clear want of a cause of action, or very clear very bad abuse of process. The remedy for want of particulars is a demand for particulars, and then (if that is not answered) a motion for particulars. The court always has the power to order further particulars, but to defer giving them until after discovery. Such a power is completely inconsistent with the idea that the pleading is liable to be struck out for mere want of particulars. Peterson v. Aperocho (1996), 199 A.R. 153 (Master), at pp. 155-56, per Master Funduk. 4. Merely Alleging a Breach of a Duty at Law Is Not Enough In Tottrup v. Alberta (Minister of Environment), 2000 ABCA 121, 2000 CarswellAlta 365, 255 A.R. 204, 81 Alta. L.R. (3d) 27, Madam Justice Conrad made it clear that it is not enough for a plaintiff to allege the breach a duty. The plaintiff must plead the facts which give rise to the alleged breach (see Rule 104). At pp. 37-38, her Ladyship said: With respect, I do not agree with my colleague, Russell J.A., that the question raised in this case should wait unit a summary judgment application before examining whether a duty could be found. She concludes that the Chambers Judge erred because, in basing his decision on the grounds that the statutes did not impose any mandatory duties on the Ministers, he failed to appreciate that the pleadings also alleged a duty “at law.” She then concedes that had the pleadings alleged only a breach of duties or powers imposed by statute, then assuming no such duties existed, the claim should be struck. But, because of the bare allegation of a “duty at law,” the claim cannot be struck. This suggests that although to plead a statutory duty is insufficient to establish a cause of action (where upon examination no such duty exists) merely alleging a duty at law will suffice, even though there are no facts pled upon which a court could conclude that such a duty at law was owing. With respect, I do not agree. In my view, it is not the allegation of a duty at law that is critical, but the facts alleged supporting such a duty. For example, a statement of claim alleging only that “A” breached a duty owed to “B” thereby causing damage does not, in my view, disclose a cause of action. Pleadings are allegations of fact and, in my view, where negligence is alleged, that allegation must be supported by facts capable of sustaining a determination that a duty was owed, that an act or omission occurred breaching that duty, and that damages resulted. On a motion to strike it is the allegations of fact that must be examined to determine whether a cause of action exists. In Al-Ghamdi v. Alberta, 2017 ABQB 684, 2017 CarswellAlta 2447, Justice Goss said: 119 Only material facts, not bare allegations, need to be taken as proven under r 3.68(2)(b): Hovsepian v Westfair Foods Ltd, 2001 ABQB 700 at paras 28-29: While the Plaintiffs state that all allegations in the Claim must be taken as proved, the Defendants propose two limits on that principle: (1) bare allegations with no facts need not be taken as proved; and (2) speculative facts or those incapable of proof need not be taken as proved. In my view, the Defendants are correct on both points. Regarding the first limitation argued by the Defendants, I agree that there is no presumption that allegations not backed by facts must be taken as proved. Bare allegations are insufficient; allegations of fact are taken as proved for purposes of the striking out test. 120 In Arabi v Alberta, 2014 ABQB 295, Gill J dealt with applications to strike an action against a panoply of defendants, and he commented on the approach to take when dealing with pleadings containing numerous and complex allegations (at pars 48, 72, and 74): Arabi's action is defective on many bases, cannot succeed, and therefore must be struck. The amorphous nature of Arabi's many allegations and the large cast of Defendants means that a detailed, point-by-point analysis is not a logistically viable process. I will therefore approach Arabi's allegations by identifying a number of general legal and factual defects that, alone and in combination, mean the Arabi Civil Action cannot legally succeed or is based on an inadequate matrix of supporting facts … In evaluation of a Rule s 3.68 application the hearing judge is to presume that the alleged facts are true. This general rule has two caveats. One is that a fact is different from a bald allegation: an allegation “… that recite[s] the basic elements of the tort in very general terms but fails to provide material facts sufficient to demonstrate an intentional wrongdoing …”: GH v Alcock, 2013 ABCA 24 at para 58. For example, Arabi's many allegations of a conspiracy among the Defendants are a bald allegation—he offers nothing on the context or details of that conspiracy … A second basis on which an alleged fact may be rejected is when it is simply an absurdity, or highly implausible. Arabi's complaints are also plagued by this defect of inherent improbability. For one, he alleges a broad-based conspiracy among lawyers involved in this matter, regardless of whether they are Crown Prosecutors or act on his behalf. (emphasis added) 5. When Limitation Period Not Expired Master Funduk has warned of the tactical error of applying to strike a statement of claim for disclosing no cause of action in instances when the plaintiff can sue again because the limitation period has not yet expired. In Jim Pattison Developments Ltd. v. Fudex International Inc. (1996), 45 Alta. L.R. (3d) 343 (Master), the learned Master said at p. 364: It never ceases to amaze me to see defendants applying to strike out a statement of claim on the ground that it does not disclose a cause of action when the limitation period for suing has not expired. If the pleading is struck out and the limitation period has not expired the plaintiff can sue again, this time with the benefit of judicial advice on what should be pled to disclose a cause of action in law. 6. Onus The onus is on the applicant. So the burden of proof lies squarely on the shoulders of the applicant, because clearly, where there is an issue, no matter how minuscule, the plaintiff should be permitted the opportunity to have the matter tried by a trial judge. Principal Group Ltd. (Trustee of) v. Alberta (1991), 118 A.R. 40 (Q.B.), at 42, per Moore C.J.Q.B. 7. Disclosing No Defence To strike out under the first ground the statement of defence must not disclose a defence in law. One cannot, under this rule, strike out a statement of defence merely because it is felt the defendant does not have a defence in fact. The rule provides that a defence can be struck out if it discloses no defence. This is not to be confused with not disclosing a reasonable defence … The pleadings should not be struck out unless it is quite clear that no defence is disclosed… Only in the clearest possible case should a pleading be struck out. Ainge v. DeCouteau (1980), 13 Alta. L.R. (2d) 193 at 194 (Master). 8. Presumption of Truth The allegations in the pleadings must be taken as true. The allegations of the statement of claim must, of course, be taken as true for the purpose of determining the question of the disclosure of a cause of action. Western Leaseholds Ltd. v. Western Minerals Ltd. (1960), 31 W.W.R. 10 at 12 (Alta. C.A.). And Côté J.A. said: On a motion to strike out for want of a cause of action, the courts assume that the plaintiff can prove the facts pleaded… Such suits go to trial, or at least to a motion for summary judgment with evidence. Galand Estate v. Stewart (1992), 6 Alta. L.R. (3d) 399 at 408 (C.A.). In Hovsepian v. Westfair Foods Ltd., 2001 ABQB 700, 2001 CarswellAlta 1113, 296 A.R. 283, 95 Alta. L.R. (3d) 331, Mr. Justice Hart noted that there are two limits on the principle that the allegations in the Statement of Claim are to be taken as proved. At pp. 342-343, His Lordship said: While the Plaintiffs state that all allegations in the Claim must be taken as proved, the Defendants propose two limits on that principle: (1) bare allegations with no facts need not be taken as proved; and (2) speculative facts or those incapable of proof need not be taken as proved. In my view, the Defendants are correct on both points. Regarding the first limitation argued by the Defendants, I agree that there is no presumption that allegations not backed by facts must be taken as proved. Bare allegations are insufficient; allegations of fact are taken as proved for purposes of the striking out test. … Regarding the second limitation argued by the Defendants, they submit that the court is not required to assume the truth of “allegations based on assumptions or speculations”, or facts that are “patently ridiculous or incapable of proof”. These phrases come, respectively, from Operation Dismantle Inc. v. R., [1985] 1 S.C.R. 441 at 455 (S.C.C.), and Air India, Re (1987), 62 O.R. (2d) 130 at 135 (Ont. H.C.). In Operation Dismantle Inc., the majority refused to consider allegations as true which were incapable of proof because they were based on assumptions or speculations as to the reactions of various governments should Canada allow the United States to test cruise missiles in Canada. The court in Air India, Re did not elaborate on its statement of “patently ridiculous”, and did not appear to need to apply that reasoning in its analysis. In Al-Ghamdi v. Alberta, 2017 ABQB 684, 2017 CarswellAlta 2447, Justice Goss said: [262] An application to strike under 3.68(2)(b) must proceed on the basis that the pleaded facts are true, unless they are manifestly incapable of proof. Those facts must also be more than bald allegations reciting the basic elements of the tort. Master Birkett quoted this statement in De Vos v. Alberta (Transportation), 2020 ABQB 234, 2020 CarswellAlta 640, 11 Alta. L.R. (7th) 97, 62 M.V.R. (7th) 237 (Master) at paragraph 47. In Broda v. Alberta, 2020 ABQB 221, 2020 CarswellAlta 623 (Master), Master Summers said: [44] Pursuant to subrule 3.68(3) of the Alberta Rules of Court no evidence may be submitted on an application under clause (b) of subrule 3.68(2). Although that subrule has been taken to mean that the statements within a plaintiff's pleading must be taken as true, there is a limit to that presumption. That is, a bare allegation, such as bad faith or malice, without any facts pled in support and without particulars, is inadequate. There is a need for descriptive evidence in support of a claim of potential wrongdoing. Nor are allegations based on assumptions or suspicions to be accepted as true: Tottrup v Alberta (Minister of Environmental Protection) 2000 ABCA 121; Walton International Group Inc v Rockyview (Municipal District No. 44), 2007 ABCA 21; G. H. v Alcock, 2013 ABCA 24; Grenon v Canada (Revenue Agency), 2017 ABCA 96; and Clark v Hunka, 2017 ABCA 346. 9. Cross-applications to Strike and Amend Claim On appeal, counsel for the respondent conceded that where there are cross-motions to strike out a statement of claim and to amend it, the judge hearing the motions should consider the amendment motion first. And it was conceded that we should look at the proposed further amended statement of claim to see if it disclosed a cause of action. United Petroleum Distributors (Calgary) Ltd. v. 548311 Alberta (1998), 65 Alta. L.R. (3d) 346 (C.A.), at 348, per curiam. In Riccioni v. Law Society of Alberta, 2017 ABQB 261, 2017 CarswellAlta 641 (Master), Master Robertson said: 36 The law is clear that when there is an application for summary judgment and there is a cross-application to amend, the Court should consider the proposed amendment before the summary judgment application: Hur v 726913 Alberta Ltd, 2013 ABQB 208 (CanLII) at para. 27 and H. Ash & Associates v Banham, 2014 ABQB 718, [2014] A.R. 731. In my view, the same approach applies to an application to strike a claim under rule 3.68. 10. Are Consent Amendments Subject to R. 3.68 Attack? During argument, the court raised the issue of whether the plaintiff was entitled to orders pursuant to rule 129 to strike those portions of the amended statement of defence and counterclaim where the allegations had been allowed to be inserted in the pleadings by the plaintiff consenting to the order granted May 15th, 1996, by Justice C.S. Phillips. Such an order would have been granted pursuant to rule 132 which authorizes the court to allow amendments. Typically the court under rule 132 would allow an amendment through the exercise of the court's discretion to allow new facts in the matter to be introduced into the pleadings to determine the real issue between the parties. On a contested motion under rule 132, the court would exercise its discretion to allow an amendment to introduce new claims and allegations where there is a possibility that the claims and allegations would be successful. Where the court had thus considered the matter under rule 132 it is unlikely that a party having opposed an amendment under rule 132 could successfully argue that the amendment once allowed had no merit under rule 129. However, as is the case here, where the parties consent to an amendment which is approved by a court order, it is possible for counsel for the plaintiff to return to court under rule 129 to have the matter struck as having no merit. In such a case, the court in the original application for an amendment had not considered any argument that part or all of the amendments were without merit. Here, previous counsel for the Bank of Montreal had consented to the amendment and present counsel having reviewed the pleadings and discovery is entitled to apply for an order pursuant to rule 129 to have the allegations struck if there is truly no merit to the allegation. Bank of Montreal v. Peddle (1998), 214 A.R. 85 (Master), at 90, per Master Laycock.

Rule 3.68(2)—“irrelevant, frivolous or improper” See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.68(2). The new rule speaks of “irrelevant”, “frivolous”, “improper”; and an “abuse of process”. Cases dealing with the concepts of “scandalous” and “vexatious” may assist in understanding “improper” and “abuse of process”. The material must show the defence to be false beyond question before the plaintiff is entitled to have it struck out… The jurisdiction to strike out a pleading should be exercised with extreme caution and only in obvious cases. Ainge v. DeCouteau, supra, at 195. And in Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. v. Prisco (1994), 158 A.R. 305 (Q.B.), Mr. Justice Forsyth said, at p. 320: Further, “vexatious” under rule 129(1)(b) of the Rules of Court does not encompass dealing with the merits of the defendants' claim. In Decock v. Alberta, 2000 ABCA 122, 2000 CarswellAlta 384, 255 A.R. 234, 79 Alta. L.R. (3d) 11; leave to appeal allowed (2000) 293 A.R. 388 (note) (S.C.C.) (notice of discontinuance filed September 10, 2001), Russell J.A. said, at p. 257: … it is difficult to conceive of a claim which discloses a cause of action and which could be considered scandalous, frivolous, vexatious, embarrassing or an abuse of process. In Dykun v. Odishaw, 2000 ABQB 548, 2000 CarswellAlta 814, 267 A.R. 318, Lee J., at pp. 326-7, said: The Ontario High Court has determined that a proceeding is vexatious if it satisfies any of the following tests: (a) the bringing of one or more actions to determine an issue which has already been determined by a court of competent jurisdiction constitutes a vexatious proceeding; (b) where it is obvious that an action cannot succeed, or if the action would lead to no possible good, or if no reasonable person can reasonably expect to obtain relief, the action is vexatious; (c) vexatious actions include those brought for an improper purpose, including the harassment and oppression of other parties by multifarious proceedings brought for purposes other than the assertion of legitimate rights; (d) it is a general characteristic of vexatious proceedings that grounds and issues raised tend to be rolled forward into subsequent actions and repeated and supplemented, often with actions brought against the lawyers who have acted for or against the litigant in earlier proceedings; (e) in determining whether proceedings are vexatious, the court must look at the whole history of the matter and not just whether there was originally a good cause of action; (f) the failure of the person instituting the proceedings to pay the costs of unsuccessful proceedings is one factor to be considered in determining whether proceedings are vexatious; (g) the respondent's conduct in persistently taking unsuccessful appeals from judicial decisions can be considered vexatious conduct of legal proceedings. Lang Michener and Fabian, Re (1987), 37 D.L.R. (4th) 685 at 691 (Ont. H.C.); Winkler v. Winkler, [1991] 2 W.W.R. 369, 70 Man. R. (2d) 47 at 374 [W.W.R.] (Q.B.); affirmed [1992] 1 W.W.R. 631, 70 Man. R. (2d) 45 (C.A.). In Jamieson v. Denman (2004), 34 Alta. L.R. (4th) 113 (Q.B.); additional reasons at (2004) 34 Alta. L.R. (4th) 162 (Q.B.), Watson J. discussed the meaning of “vexatious” At pp 148-149, his Lordship said (footnotes omitted): I consider the word “vexatious” to carry with it a normative concept as well as a legal one. It seems to me that a party can be said to have acted in a vexatious manner, not merely that they acted in a manner which might be characterized as mean-spirited or nasty, but also that in fact the nastiness conveyed itself through to the legal process itself. In other words, that the legal process was being misused. My view of the word “vexatious” is that it connotes not simply that the party was acting without the highest of motives, or was acting in a manner which was hostile towards the other side. “Vexatious”, as a word, means to me that the litigant's mental state goes beyond simple animus against the other side, and rises to a situation where the litigant actually is attempting to abuse or misuse the legal process. This form of a normative component arises because it seems to me that proceedings which are legally possible or procedurally allowable may still be “vexatious” under my definition of the word “vexatious” for this purpose. In other words, mere bad or selfish motive might not be sufficient to establish vexatiousness. On the other hand, bad or selfish motive might likewise not be absolutely necessary to establish vexatiousness although it seems likely that bad or selfish motives would tend to co-exist with using the legal process in bad faith and vexatiously. As to the term “frivolous”, Justice Acton said at p. 160 of Haljan v. Serdahely Estate, 2008 ABQB 472, 2008 CarswellAlta 1028, 453 A.R. 337, 93 Alta. L.R. (4th) 151: 21 The Plaintiff argues that the term “frivolous” has not been defined anywhere, but connotes humour or mirth, and is “something that would make a lawyer or judge laugh.” Contrary to what the Plaintiff has alleged, the term has been defined. In Can. (M.C.I.) v. Seifert (2002), 221 F.T.R. 228 at paras. 10 and 11, the court stated: A frivolous plea is one so palpably bad that the Court needs no real argument to be convinced of that fact. Indeed, a frivolous plea is indicative of bad faith. Frivolous and vexatious pleas include those brought or carried on by a party who is not acting bona fide. Indeed it is a proceeding which will lead to no practical result. The concepts of frivolous and vexatiousness define the obviously unsustainable claim: see Attorney General of Duchy of Lancaster v. London and North Western Railway Co., [1892] 3 Ch. 274 at 277 (C.A.). The frivolous and vexatious pleading includes those which are an abuse of process: Ashmore v. British Coal Corp., [1990] 2 Q.B. 338 at 347 (C.A.). 22 The court in 876502 Ont. Inc. v. Propco Holdings (1997), 49 O.T.C. 356, ¶ 18 (Gen. Div.) indicated that: A frivolous action has been defined, however, to be one which, on its face, is so unreal that no reasonable or sensible person could bring it. A frivolous and vexatious pleading has been defined as one which is “hopeless factually”, and which it is “plain and obvious … cannot succeed”. Excelsior Life Insurance Co. v. Zurich Investments Ltd. and Drucker et al. (1988), 89 A.R. 14, 59 Alta. L.R. (2d) 209, 28 C.P.C. (2d) 264 (C.A.) 23 Frivolous also has been defined in several legal dictionaries: Dictionary of Canadian Law, 3rd ed. (Scarborough: Thomson Carswell, 2004): frivolous: lacking in substance, Gouge v. Halliday (1919), 14 Alta. L.R. 296 (Alta. S.C.) frivolous and vexatious: said of a pleading which is hopeless factually and plainly cannot succeed in its purpose. Stroud's Judicial Dictionary of Words and Phrases, 6th ed. (London: Sweet & Maxwells, 2000) frivolous: futile, misconceived, hopeless or academic. Black's Law Dictionary, 8th ed. (St. Paul: Thomson West, 2004) frivolous: lacking a legal basis or legal merit; not serious, not reasonably purposeful.

Rule 3.68(2)(c)—“irrelevant” or “improper” See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.68(2)(c). If a pleading is relevant it is not prejudicial or embarrassing. Ainge v. De Couteau, supra, at 195. This statement was specifically approved by Wachowich A.C.J.Q.B. in Lytton v. Alberta (1999), 245 A.R. 282 at 287-88 (Q.B.). The Saskatchewan Court of Appeal said: The term “embarrassing” has been defined many times and in London (Mayor) v. Horner (1914), 3 LTR 512 at 514 … Pickford, L.J. stated as follows: I take ‘embarrassing’ to mean that the allegations are so irrelevant that to allow them to stand would involve useless expenses and would also prejudice the trial of the action by involving the parties in a dispute that is wholly apart from the issues. Meyers v. Freeholders Oil Co. (1956), 19 W.W.R. 546 at 549 (Sask. C.A.). In Alberta, Master Funduk has said: The fact that allegations by a plaintiff in her pleading may be personally embarrassing to a defendant is not of itself a ground to strike the pleading. No doubt some defendants will find the allegations against them to be personally embarrassing, particularly so if the allegations are not true. However, defendants cannot short circuit lawsuits because of their personal feelings. Embarrassing means unreasonable and prejudicial. This part of the Rule is designed to enforce intelligibility and the rules of pleadings …Holloway v. Alberta Pork Producers Development Corp. (1996), 40 Alta. L.R. (3d) 312 (Master), at 317, per Master Funduk. With respect to a counterclaim in which the claiming party seeks the same relief as is sought in another action, Power J. said in Balm v. BHC Securities Inc., 2003 ABQB 773, 2003 CarswellAlta 1301, 350 A.R. 379, at p. 384: Where a defendant files a counterclaim for relief which is the duplicate of relief being sought in a separate, earlier action, the relief should be decided in the original action and the counterclaim should be struck on the basis that the identical issue had already been raised by the defendant in the first action. Marcels Truck Service Ltd. v. Karnoth Transportation & Construction (1988) Ltd., [1993] A.J. No. 256, 142 A.R. 390 at p. 3 [A.J.] (Q.B. Master). Moore C.J.Q.B. has said: “Embarrassing” may include pleading motive, depending on the facts of the case: Schreiner v. Hamre (1980), 5 Sask. R. 76 (C.A.). Mikisew Cree First Nation v. Canada (1997), 214 A.R. 194 (Q.B.), at 196, per Moore C.J.Q.B. Can one apply under R. 129(b) or (c) after demanding particulars? Master Breitkreuz is of the view that one cannot: … a party who serves a demand for particulars has conceded the relevance of the allegations in respect of which particulars are demanded. In my view the demand for particulars has foreclosed the issue of relevance, and it appears to be clear that regardless of how embarrassing the pleading may be in the every day use of the word “embarrassing”, it is not legally embarrassing if it is relevant. It appears that an “embarrassing” pleading in the context of R. 129, is simply a pleading of a fact, the proof of which will not be determinative in the outcome, one way or the other. Creswell v. Edmonton Journal (1986), 42 Alta. L.R. (2d) 395 at 396 (Master). Master Waller takes a different view. In Valentine v. Bee-Bell Health Bakery Ltd. (1993), 161 A.R. 1 (Master), Master Waller said at pp. 2-3: The respondent initially argues that the mere fact that the applicant has demanded particulars with respect to the impugned paragraphs, forecloses any argument that such paragraphs should be struck. He relies upon the authority of Creswell v. Edmonton Journal… With respect, I cannot agree with this view taken by my learned colleague. The purpose of the rules relating to the furnishing of further and better particulars is to limit the generality of the pleadings with a view to have the prior pleading made sufficiently distinct to enable the applicant to frame his answer thereto properly: per Boyd, C., in Smith v. Boyd (1897), 17 P.R. 463 at p. 467. Particulars once furnished [form] part of the pleadings, Millbank v. Millbank, [1990] 1 Ch. 376 at p. 385. A requirement that a plaintiff define his claim does not of necessity admit to the relevance of the claim. Indeed particulars may properly be required as a necessary step to define the claim for a striking action. The respondent must fail in this argument.

Rule 3.68(2)(d)—Abuse of process See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.68(2)(d). 1. Not a Closed Category In J.A. Industries (Canada) Ltd. v. Highfield Development Ltd. (1998), 67 Alta. L.R. (3d) 349, 1998 CarswellAlta 896, 230 A.R. 71, 67 Alta. L.R. (3d) 349 (Master), Master Funduk said, at p. 360: Abuse of process is not a closed category: Hurley v. Co-operators General Insurance Co. (1998), 160 D.L.R. (4th) 645 (N.S.C.A.). There the Court says, pp. 658-59: For the purpose of this appeal, it is neither necessary, nor desirable, to define, or to limit, the phrase ‘abuse of the process of the court’, as that phrase is used in Civil Procedure Rule 14.25. It is sufficient to note, only, that the phrase, in the context of rule 14.25, contemplates that, in commencing, or maintaining, a legal proceeding, the process of the court is being misused, or is being used for an improper purpose; as opposed to an action being brought, or maintained, for the assertion of legitimate rights. In Trimove Inc. v. Servus Credit Union, 2017 ABQB 50, 2017 CarswellAlta 88, 44 C.B.R. (6th) 5, Justice Nielsen said: 43 The Supreme Court of Canada considered the doctrine of abuse of process in its decision in Behn v Moulton Contracting Ltd, 2013 SCC 26, [2013] 2 SCR 227: 40 The doctrine of abuse of process is characterized by its flexibility. Unlike the concepts of res judicata and issue estoppel, abuse of process is unencumbered by specific requirements. In Canam Enterprises Inc. v. Coles (2000), 51 O.R. (3d) 481 (C.A.), Goudge J.A., who was dissenting, but whose reasons this Court subsequently approved (2002 SCC 63, [2002] 3 S.C.R. 307), stated at paras. 55-56 that the doctrine of abuse of process engages the inherent power of the court to prevent the misuse of its procedure, in a way that would be manifestly unfair to a party to the litigation before it or would in some other way bring the administration of justice into disrepute. It is a flexible doctrine unencumbered by the specific requirements of concepts such as issue estoppel. See House of Spring Gardens Ltd. v. Waite, [1990] 3 W.L.R. 347 [(C.A.)], at p. 358 … One circumstance in which abuse of process has been applied is where the litigation before the court is found to be in essence an attempt to relitigate a claim which the court has already determined. See Solomon v. Smith, supra. It is on that basis that Nordheimer J. found that this third party claim ought to be terminated as an abuse of process. [Emphasis added.] In Al-Ghamdi v. Alberta, 2017 ABQB 684, 2017 CarswellAlta 2447, Justice Goss said: 123 Under r. 3.68(2)(c), a commencement document or pleading that is frivolous, irrelevant or improper may be struck. Further under r 3.68(2)(d), a commencement document or pleading that constitutes an abuse of process may also be struck. In Arabi, the Court noted that the concepts of abuse of process and frivolous and vexatious litigation are related (at para 89), citing R v Scott, [1990] 3 SCR 979 at 1007. Although r 3.68(2)(c) no longer mentions vexatious, litigation, Alberta courts have continued to strike out vexatious litigation under either r 3.68(2)(c) or (d) because “vexatious” can be said to be the same thing as impropriety and abuse of process: McMeekin v Alberta (Attorney General), 2012 ABQB 144, at para 11; Wong v. Leung, 2011 ABQB 688 at para 33. 2. Defending an Action Defending an action cannot of itself be an abuse of the process of the court. The plaintiff must make out that the defendant is using the process of the court against good faith and not bona fide. Ainge v. DeCouteau (1980) 13 Alta. L.R. 193 at 198 (Master). 3. Inherent Power of Court Aside entirely from the Rules of Court there is, I think, inherent jurisdiction vested in the court to strike out a statement of claim as being plainly an abuse of the process of the court. Poitras v. Alberta (Attorney General) (1969), 68 W.W.R. 224 at 227 Alta. T.D. 4. Court Does Not Presume Truth of Pleadings Unlike applications under R. 129(1)(a), when considering an application under R. 129(1)(d) the court will not presume that the allegations in the pleadings are true. Of course, on an application under subr. 1(a) of R. 129, to strike out a statement of claim because it discloses no cause of action, the court must take the allegations in the statement of claim as true … The court assumes that the plaintiff can prove the facts pleaded … However, we are not concerned here with an application under subr. 1(a)… We are here concerned with an application under subr. 1(d), to strike the statement of claim or dismiss the action on the ground of abuse of process… However, in relation to an application under subr. 1(d), [the learned Chambers judge] was not entitled to take the allegations in the statement of claim as true. Boudreault v. Barrett (1995), 33 Alta. L.R. (3d) 60 (C.A.), at 65, per curiam. 5. Court Can Consider All the Pleadings In Lonrho v. Fayed (No. 2), [1991] 4 All E.R. 961 (Ch. Div.) Millet, J., commented on the evidence which he was permitted to consider in respect of an application to strike out a statement of claim. He said that where the application to strike is based on the claim that it discloses no reasonable cause of action, absolutely no outside evidence may be noted. The Judge looks only to the statement of claim to determine whether it sets out a cause of action. It is quite different for an application to strike out a statement of claim on the ground that it is vexatious or an abuse of process. In this case, evidence is admissible to show that the claim is vexatious or an abuse of process. “Unless the defendant can demonstrate shortly and conclusively that the plaintiff's claim is bound to fail or is otherwise objectionable as an abuse of process of the court, it must be allowed to proceed to trial” (at 965). The Court said, “I am entitled and bound to have regard, not only to Lonrho's pleaded case and the evidence available to support it, but also to the history of the dispute.” (at 966). . . . . . … in determining whether proceedings are vexatious, the court must look at the whole history of the matter and not just whether there was originally a good cause of action. From my consideration of these cases, I am satisfied that I am entitled to look not only at the present statement of claim but the other pleadings surrounding the plaintiff's occupation of the condominium to gain a view of the history of the dispute. Osborne v. Pinno (1997), 208 A.R. 363 (Q.B.), at pp. 366-67, per Marshall J. 6. Ulterior Motive; Collateral Advantage I turn directly to consideration of whether the pleading is an abuse of process. There is a paucity of authority from Alberta respecting abuse of process. Goldsmith v. Sperrings Ltd., [1977] 2 All E.R. 556 (C.A.) was a civil libel action brought by a businessman who was the subject of unflattering articles in a satirical magazine. He brought the action against secondary distributors of the magazine. Some of those settled, but the remaining parties brought a motion to strike the pleadings on the ground that they had not been brought bona fide for proper purposes but were an abuse of the process… Lord Justice Bridge stated: In my judgment, one can certainly go so far as to say that when a litigant sues to redress a grievance no object which he may seek to obtain can be condemned as a collateral advantage if it is reasonably related to the provision of some form of redress for that grievance. On the other hand, if it can be shown that a litigant is pursuing an ulterior purpose unrelated to the subject matter of the litigation and that, but for his ulterior purpose he would not have commenced proceedings at all, that is an abuse of process. Lord Justice Scarman stated at 582: In the instant proceedings the defendants have to show that the plaintiff has an ulterior motive, seeks a collateral advantage for himself beyond what the law offers, is reaching out ‘to effect an object not within the scope of the process’. Osborne v. Pinno (1997), 208 A.R. 363 (Q.B.), at p. 366, per Marshall J. 7. Where Second Action Constitutes Abuse of Process A second action which is continuing while the first still exists is an abuse of process. … it [is] plainly an abuse to allow a second action to continue while the other is in good standing… The test in these matters was set out… under the following two conditions: 1. Continuance of the action would work an injustice because it would be oppressive or vexatious or an abuse of process in some other way, and; 2. The stay must not cause an injustice to the plaintiff. The burden of proof of both these conditions is on the person asking for the stay. The word oppressive has been legally defined as usually referring to deliberate acts of moral, although not necessarily legal, delinquency such as an unfair abuse of power by the stronger party in order that a weaker party may be put in difficulties in obtaining his just rights. Vexatious was said to involve overtones of an irresponsible pursuit of litigation by someone who either knows he has no proper cause of action or is mentally incapable of forming a rational opinion on the topic. It has been suggested that a liberal interpretation of what is vexatious and oppressive ought to be adopted and the court has stated that either attitude amounted to an abuse of process. See Mohler v. Dairy Queen of Western Canada Ltd. et al., [1976] 3 W.W.R. 620, an Alberta Appellate Division case … Abuse of process clearly applies where there is a multiplicity of proceedings, such as two or more law suits for virtually the same matter. Whitehead v. Taber (1983), 46 A.R. 14 at 16 (Q.B.). And in Edmonton Northlands v. Edmonton Oilers Hockey Corp. (1993), 15 Alta. L.R. (3d) 179 (Q.B.), Moore C.J.Q.B. said at pp. 185-86: The courts of Alberta generally recognize a rule against multiple prosecution. It is trite law that commencing a second action while one is currently pending is an abuse of process: German v. Major (1985), 39 Alta. L.R. (2d) 270 (C.A.). Since the same relief can be obtained in the first action, Northlands is not entitled to bring a second action while the first is still pending: Great Pacific Contracting Ltd. v. Harwyn Properties (1981), 29 B.C.L.R. 145 (S.C.). In my view, the second action must be set aside. If the first action has been dismissed for want of prosecution, then a second action is not an abuse of process. This argument evades the fundamental issue, which is whether a second lawsuit is an abuse of process if a prior lawsuit for the same cause of action is effectively dismissed for want of prosecution. The present answer to that, in Alberta, is no. Birkett v. James, [1978] A.C. 297 (H.L.), and Department of Transport v. Chris Smaller (Transport) Ltd., [1989] 2 W.L.R. 578 (H.L.), say that if a first lawsuit is dismissed for want of prosecution the plaintiff can sue again. The dismissal of the first lawsuit for want of prosecution is not a bar to a second lawsuit. Res judicata does not apply. Birkett and Department of Transport were accepted in Alberta Government Telephones v. Arrow Excavators & Trenchers (1972) Ltd. (1989), 69 Alta. L.R. (2d) 332 (C.A.) (“A.G.T.”). In that case there was inordinate delay, the delay was inexcusable and the defendant was likely to be seriously prejudiced by the delay. Without more, the lawsuit should have been dismissed. It was not because the court said that the plaintiff could just sue again. The result would have been different if the plaintiff could not have sued again. Birkett addresses the issue whether it is an abuse of process to start a second lawsuit if the first lawsuit is dismissed for want of prosecution. It says that it is not. Department of Transport refused to depart from Birkett in any way and the second case has been followed by A.G.T. Sinclair Timber Industries Ltd. v. Métis Assn. Regional Council—Zone No. 1 (1995), 31 Alta. L.R. (3d) 279 (Master), at 281-82, per Master Funduk. With respect to a counterclaim in which the claiming party seeks the same relief as is sought in another action, Power J. said in Balm v. BHC Securities Inc., 2003 ABQB 773, 2003 CarswellAlta 1301, 350 A.R. 379, at p. 384: Where a defendant files a counterclaim for relief which is the duplicate of relief being sought in a separate, earlier action, the relief should be decided in the original action and the counterclaim should be struck on the basis that the identical issue had already been raised by the defendant in the first action. Marcels Truck Service Ltd. v. Karnoth Transportation & Construction (1988) Ltd., [1993] A.J. No. 256, 142 A.R. 390 at p. 3 [A.J.] (Q.B. Master). 8. Res Judicata Principal seeks to strike the statement of claim on the basis that all issues raised in this matter had been previously finally determined by a court of competent jurisdiction. The principle of res judicata applies to bar repetitive continuing litigation on the same cause of action. It applies to issues of law and fact which were the subject matter of express judicial determination in an action between the same parties. It applies also to matters which were not specifically dealt with, but which must implicitedly [sic] have been decided because the decision could not have been made without a determination of that issue. Finally, all matters which should have been raised but which were not raised in defence of the action (with certain exceptions) are barred once a final decision is granted. Malik v. Principal Savings & Trust Co. (1985), 63 A.R. 109 (Q.B.), at 113, per McFadyen J. And Kerans J.A. said: Res judicata can extend to matters that ought to have been raised; it is not restricted to issues actually determined on the merits. Terroco Industries Ltd. v. Viking Oilfield Supply Ltd. (1987), 57 Alta. L.R. (2d) 62 at 64 (C.A.). Côté J.A. has said: It suffices to dispose of this suit to say that any and all of the matters now raised, reasonably could have been raised at the latest, in the 1984 suit by the village against the same parties. (If any could not, then that would only be because they should have been raised in the first suit.) Res judicata is not limited to what was argued and decided in the previous suit. It extends to what reasonably should have been raised. Litigation by instalments is interminable. Argentia Beach (Summer Village) v. Warshawski (1991), 84 Alta. L.R (2d) 202 at 203 (C.A.). In 420093 B.C. Ltd. v. Bank of Montreal (1995), 34 Alta. L.R. (3d) 269 (C.A.), the Court of Appeal considered the topic of res judicata. At pp. 276-77, Mr. Justice O'Leary, speaking for the court, said: Estoppel by res judicata is a rule of evidence. Where a final judicial decision has been pronounced by a court of competent jurisdiction over the parties and the subject matter “… any party or privy to such litigation, as against any other party or privy thereto, and in the case of a decision in rem, any person whatsoever, as against any other person, is estopped in any subsequent litigation from disputing or questioning such decision on the merits”: Spencer Bower and Turner, The Doctrine of Res Judicata (2nd ed.), at p. 9. The two forms of estoppel by res judicata are described in Sopinka, Lederman and Bryant, The Law of Evidence in Canada, at p. 997. The first is commonly called “issue estoppel” and is defined as follows: … any action or issue which has been litigated and upon which a decision has been rendered cannot be refuted in a subsequent suit between the same parties or their privies. This principle prevents the contradiction of that which was determined in the previous litigation, by prohibiting the relitigation of issues already actually addressed. [Emphasis in original] The second is “cause of action estoppel”: The second principle makes it mandatory that a plaintiff asserting a cause of action must claim all possible relief in respect thereto and prevents any second attempt to invoke the aid of the courts in the same cause. It is sometimes called ‘merger’ because the plaintiff's cause of action becomes ‘merged’ in the judgment. The judgment actually operates as a comprehensive declaration of the rights of all parties in respect of the matters in issue. As a result, the rule applies equally to a defendant who must put forward all defences which will defeat the plaintiff's action, and the defendant who does not will be debarred from raising them subsequently. This principle prevents the fragmentation of litigation by prohibiting the litigation of matters that were never actually addressed in the previous litigation, but which properly belonged to it. [Emphasis in original] A prior judicial decision will not raise an estoppel by res judicata, either issue estoppel or cause of action estoppel, unless (i) it was a final decision pronounced by a court of competent jurisdiction over the parties and the subject matter; (ii) the decision was, or involved, a determination of the same issue or cause of action as that sought to be controverted or advanced in the present litigation; and (iii) the parties to the prior judicial proceeding or their privies are the same persons as the parties to the present action or their privies. The court in 420093 B.C. Ltd. v. Bank of Montreal, at pp. 286-87, then made the following comments about abuse of process: The Court of Queen's Bench has power under R. 129 and its inherent jurisdiction to strike out an action as an abuse of process. The power is discretionary and its exercise will not be interfered with on appeal unless it was unreasonable. An attempt to re-litigate issues already decided or deemed to have been decided may be found an abuse of process and barred in circumstances where estoppel by res judicata is not available, for example where only one of the parties to the later action was a party to the earlier one … In Solomon v. Smith (1987), [1988] 1 W.W.R. 410 … the Manitoba Court of Appeal struck out an action on the ground that it was an abuse of process in circumstances where estoppel by res judicata was not applicable. In language apt to the case at Bar, Lyon J.A., said at p. 421: I agree … that a plea of issue estoppel is not available. However to permit the statement of claim to proceed would be an abuse of process and that is the principle applicable. In considering this doctrine, it seems to me prudent to avoid hard and fast, institutionalized rules such as those which attach to the plea of issue estoppel. By encouraging the determination of each case on its own facts against the general principle of the plea of abuse, serious prejudice to either party as well as the proper administration of justice can best be avoided … we must be vigilant to ensure that the system does not become unnecessarily clogged with repetitious litigation of the kind here attempted. There should be an end to this litigation. To allow the plaintiff to retry the issue of misrepresentation would be a classic example of abuse of process—a waste of time and resources of litigants and the court and an erosion of the principle of finality so crucial to the proper administration of justice. In Wavel Ventures Corp. v. Constantini (1996), 46 Alta. L.R. (3d) 292, the Court of Appeal again had before it the issue of res judicata. Having referred with approval to O'Leary J.A.'s decision in 420093 B.C. Ltd. v. Bank of Montreal (1995), 34 Alta. L.R. (3d) 269 (C.A.), McFadyen J.A. said at pp. 306-307: The rule of res judicata is not absolute in application. In some limited circumstances, a party may be permitted to enter upon new proceedings which contest a decision of an earlier court, even if the tests stated above are met. One such exception occurs when fraud is practised upon the court… In Canada, the test to be met by a party seeking to establish that exception to res judicata was stated by Garrow J. in Jacobs v. Beaver (1908), 17 O.L.R. 496 at 506 (C.A.). The fraud relied on must be something collateral or extraneous, and not merely the fraud which is imputed from alleged false statements made at the trial, which were met by counter-statements by the other side, and the whole adjudicated upon by the court and so passed on into the limbo of estoppel by the judgment. This estoppel cannot be disturbed except upon the allegation and proof of new and material facts, and from which are to be deduced the proposition that the former judgment was obtained by fraud. ..... A second exception to the res judicata principle may apply on the discovery of new evidence. That exception, however, is very limited in scope. It is not the simple acquisition of fresh evidence which permits a party to escape the consequences of the principle of res judicata. Ritchie J. in Grandview (Town) v. Doering, [1976] S.C.R. 621 at p. 636 adopted the following passage from the decision of the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal in Fenerty v. Halifax (City) (1920), 53 NS.R. 457 C.A., at 463: The doctrine of res judicata is founded on public policy so that there may be an end of litigation, and also to prevent the hardship to the individual of being twice vexed by the same cause. The rule which I deduce from the authorities is that a judgment between the same parties is final and conclusive not only as to the matters dealt with, but also as to questions which the parties had the opportunity of raising. It is clear that the plaintiff must go forward in the first suit with his evidence; he will not be permitted in the event of a failure to proceed with a second suit on the ground that he has additional evidence. In order to be at liberty to proceed with a second suit he must be prepared to say: I will show you this is a fact which entirely changes the aspect of the case, and I will show you further that it was not, and could not by reasonable diligence have been ascertained by me before. (Emphasis added) In Escobar v. Yacey (1998), 229 A.R. 278 (Q.B.), Madam Justice Johnstone discussed res judicata as it applies to settlements between the parties. At p. 284, Her Ladyship said: The House of Lords in Jenkin v. Robertson, [1867] L.R. 1 Sc. & Div. 117 (H.L.) … held that a compromise, agreement or such arrangement of the parties, without judicial examination of its merits, cannot form the basis of res judicata. This decision was followed in Hair v. Meaford (Town) (1914), 31 O.L.R. 124 (C.A.) and illustrates the distinction between a court acting in an administrative capacity or acting in a more explicitly judicial capacity. Lord Romilly in Jenkin… referred to the meaning of res judicata as a judicial pronouncement. Lord Romilly stated the requirement …“the court has exercised its judicial mind, and has come to the conclusion that the one side or the other side is right, and has pronounced a decision accordingly.” If the court simply “registers” the agreement of the parties, res judicata cannot be invoked on the basis of that agreement. . . . . . An order of the court can be distinguished from a contract between or among parties which may be deemed a “settlement agreement”. Master Funduk, in Angeltvedt v. Lawes et al. (1994), 164 A.R. 201 (Q.B. Master), stated that settlement agreements are not “judgments”. In that case, the determination of the status of the settlement was relevant in determining the responsibilities of the third party once the issue between the plaintiff and the defendant had been settled. A settlement agreement of that kind is in a different category than those that are taken to the court to be affixed with the court's imprimatur. If such occurs, the agreement of the parties has been transformed into a decision of the court. The status of consent agreements as final judgments has been noted in the cases of Bank of Montreal v. Coopers Lybrand Inc. and Ostapowich (1996), 144 Sask. R. 207 (C.A.) and Wensel v. Wensel et al. (1975), 65 D.L.R. (3d) 327 (Alta. T.D.). In the first case, the court definitively states that a consent judgment is a “final decision of the court.” A consent agreement is not simply approved by the court as a formality, but is addressed independently by the court, before it receives its status as a judgment. In 688560 Alberta Ltd. v. Genesis Land Developers Ltd., 2000 CarswellAlta 203, 82 Alta. L.R. (3d) 236, Verville J., at pp. 241-242, said: The doctrine of res judicata is defined succinctly in Schacher v. National Bailiff Services (January 20, 1999), Doc. Edmonton 9603-18327, 9703-11746 (Alta. Q.B.), at para. 27: The Common (sic) law doctrine of estoppel by res judicata is a rule of evidence. Where a final decision has been pronounced by a court of competent jurisdiction over the parties to, and the subject of, the litigation, any party or privy to such litigation, as against any other party or privy thereto is estopped in any subsequent litigation from disputing or questioning such decision on the merits, whether it be used as the foundation of an action, or relied upon as a bar to any claim, indictment or complaint, or to any affirmative defence, case, or allegation. … … Lee J. in Schacher, … states: The true test then of the doctrine of res judicata is identity of issue. The question is whether or not the judgment is conclusive, not merely as to the point actually decided but as to any matter which it was necessary to decide and which was actually decided as the groundwork of the decision itself, though not directly the point at issue. The Court is entitled to look at the pleadings, the reasons for judgment and the formal judgment to determine with precision, the issues decided. 9. Collateral attack and abuse of process In Trimove Inc. v. Servus Credit Union, 2017 ABQB 50, 2017 CarswellAlta 88, 44 C.B.R. (6th) 5, Trimove sued Servus Credit Union alleging that Servus breached the loan agreements it had with Trimove when Servus appointed a receiver and liquidated assets of Trimove. Servus applied for an order striking out the Statement of Claim on the grounds that it did not disclose a cause of action, it constituted a collateral attack on the receivership order, and was an abuse of process. Justice Nielsen struck part of the Statement of Claim, and gave this summary of the law relating to applications to strike pleadings in such circumstances: 68 I note that most of the above cases involved applications for summary judgment. Nevertheless, a number of the general principles flowing from them are relevant to this application to strike pleadings: 1. the principle of collateral attack generally makes an order of a court having jurisdiction binding and conclusive, and not susceptible to attack in a proceeding where the object of that proceeding is other than the reversal, variation or nullification of the order or judgment: Behn, Nash 2. if an order is obtained by fraud, non-disclosure or misleading disclosure, it can be challenged directly by an application to set it aside or by appeal, but not collaterally: Got, McDonald 3. a lender may be liable where it improperly obtained a receivership order, for example, where: (a) the lender seeks both a preservation and realization order on the same day as it issues its demand for repayment, with no explanation as to why little notice was given, nor any indication of a cause for urgency or inability of the debtor to pay the debt: Got (b) the lender misleads the Court in relation to its communications with the debtor in relation to enforcing its security, and the risk to recovery: Got 4. a borrower may raise an allegation that the lender reneged on a forbearance agreement in response to an application for the appointment of a receiver: Tassone 5. a challenge to the propriety of an ex parte receivership order may be brought by way of a counterclaim in the receivership action: Got, McDonald 6. a post-receivership action against a lender is a collateral attack on orders granted in the receivership proceedings if those orders were not appealed: Got, McDonald 7. a post-receivership defence to a claim for deficiency by the lender is not barred by issue estoppel or estoppel by conduct if the defence is based on the bank's conduct prior to the proceedings to appoint a receiver: Ross 8. in considering the failure to challenge decisions in a receivership, a court may take into account that the speedy sale of assets may be in everyone's interests in order to minimize the potential loss due to an allegedly improper interim receiver order, and that a trial would significantly slow down the fulfillment of the receiver's mandate set in motion by that interim order: Ross 9. where the debtor does not appeal the receivership order, subsequent claims that the lender's actions led to the loan default and that the receiver improperly disposed of the project are belated collateral attacks (absent proven fraud) if the essence of the proposed claims would directly conflict with aspects of the receivership and sale orders: Cheema 10. failure to appeal or to apply to set aside or vary a receivership order will not bar a viable claim against the lender where attempts were made to appeal the receivership orders within the proper time period, and counsel agreed the debtor could raise the allegations contained in the statement of defence and counterclaim in the receivership action as a defence in the trial of a subsequent action by the lender for outstanding indebtedness: Got, Nahal 11. a post-receivership suit against a lender is hopeless and cannot possibly benefit an insolvent debtor unless it can yield a cash recovery exceeding the debtor's debt to the lender, as any recovery up to that sum would merely reduce the insolvent debtor's debts: Cheema 12. it is an error to strike post-receivership pleadings as an abuse of process if the pleadings, evidence and parties' agreements in the record are unclear as to relevant circumstances in the receivership proceedings: Ross.

Rule 3.68 is used when parties are attempting to have part of a claim or defence struck, a document or pleading amended or set aside, to enter judgment or an order, or to stay an action, application or proceeding. Rule 3.68(2) outlines the conditions required.
3.68(3), no evidence is permitted on whether a reasonable claim has been pleaded within the meaning of rule 3.68(2)(b). Quaye v. Law Society of Alberta, [2021] A.J. No. 629, 2021 ABCA 167 at para. 13 (Alta. C.A.); Parenteau v. Spencer, [2023] A.J. No. 988, 2023 ABCA 268 at para. 9 (Alta. C.A.). The plaintiff is entitled to a broad reading of the pleadings. PricewaterhouseCoopers Inc. v. Perpetual Energy Inc., [2021] A.J. No. 84, 2021 ABCA 16 at para. 74 (Alta. C.A.); , [2012] A.J. Alberta Adolescent Recovery Centre v. Canadian Broadcasting Corp. No. 61, 2012 ABQB 48 at para. 25 (Alta. Q.B.); Harun-ar-Rashid v. Canada (Royal Canadian Mounted Police), [2019] A.J. No. 84, 2019 ABQB 54 at paras. 14, 18 (Alta. Q.B.).
However, bare assertions or allegations are insufficient, and the failure to provide facts to substantiate a reasonable claim is grounds for striking the claim under this rule. Quaye v Law Society of Alberta, [2021] A.J. No. 629, 2021 ABCA 167 at para. 13 (Alta. C.A.); Rana v. Baker Gay v. Alberta (Workers’ , [2022] A.J. No. 632, 2022 ABCA 180 at para. 8 (Alta. C.A.); Essential R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd.
